narrative:
The model determined that you have a 59.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was significantly weaker than most successful applicants.

Next, your family income bracket worked in the opposite direction. Coming from a lower-middle income family actually made the model slightly more optimistic about your chances, since this background is relatively uncommon among accepted students and the model treated it as a mild positive factor.

Your LSAT score was the third most important element and pulled the prediction back toward failure. Scoring 24 is well below the average of 37 among accepted students, and this gap contributed noticeably to the higher risk of not passing the bar.

Taken together, your low third-year ranking and modest LSAT score outweighed the small positive effect from your family background, leading to the denial.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Strengthening those two areas would most directly improve your chances in a future application. (248 words)
